propositions.text: The Appellant is a Pakistani citizen appealing the RPD's denial of refugee protection.
The Appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and refer for redetermination by a different panel.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant, a Pakistani citizen, appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection and asks the RAD to set aside and refer the matter back.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence to that arising after claim rejection or not reasonably available before.

paragraphs.summary: Section 110(4) IRPA restricts new evidence to that arising after claim rejection or not reasonably available before, stated by law.

propositions.text: The Appellant tendered three documents as new evidence: affidavits from sister-in-law, daughter, and a statutory declaration from brother.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted three documents as new evidence: affidavits from sister-in-law, daughter, and brother's statutory declaration.

propositions.text: The daughter's affidavit dated April 9, 2015 does not meet section 110(4) IRPA as it concerns events before the hearing and was reasonably available then.
The daughter's affidavit will not be accepted as new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the daughter's affidavit does not meet section 110(4) IRPA and will not accept it as new evidence.

propositions.text: The sister-in-law's affidavit dated April 6, 2015 about an attack on the Appellant's father is accepted as new evidence under section 110(4) IRPA.
This new evidence would not cause the RAD to set aside the credibility determination or change the decision.
The evidence is not relevant to the claim's determination as documentation about the attack was submitted and addressed at the RPD hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts the sister-in-law's affidavit as new evidence but finds it irrelevant and not affecting credibility or decision.

propositions.text: The brother's affidavit dated April 9, 2015 about family separation and danger to the Appellant could have been presented before the hearing and is not accepted as new evidence.
Point 7 of the brother's affidavit, about an event after the hearing, is accepted as new evidence but is not relevant or sufficient to change the credibility determination.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects most of the brother's affidavit as new evidence except Point 7, which is accepted but irrelevant to credibility or decision.

propositions.text: The brother's statement about the Appellant's husband attacking his father lacks indication of source or eyewitness evidence.
The affidavit does not raise a determinative credibility issue and is not relevant under section 110(6)(b),(c).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the brother's affidavit lacks probative support and is not relevant to credibility or determinative issues.

propositions.text: Because the new evidence does not meet criteria, no oral hearing will be held.

paragraphs.summary: The court decides no oral hearing will be held as the new evidence does not meet criteria.

propositions.text: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under section 111(1)(a) IRPA.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges the Board erred by failing to apply Gender Guidelines.
The Appellant alleges error in the Board's treatment of supporting evidence.
The Appellant alleges the Board was unreasonable in its credibility determination.
The Appellant alleges error in finding her account of former spouse's actions not plausible.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges errors in applying Gender Guidelines, treating evidence, credibility, and plausibility of spouse's actions.

propositions.text: The Appellant is a female Shia Muslim from Pakistan with moderate views.
Her husband became more religious and controlling after attending a Wahabi mosque in 2012, beating her and demanding conversion.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant is a Shia Muslim woman whose husband became more religious and abusive after attending a Wahabi mosque.

propositions.text: In 2013, the husband assaulted and threatened the Appellant, demanding conversion and removal of children from English school.
The Appellant fled, went into hiding, got a Canadian visa, and claimed refugee protection; RPD rejected claim in 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant was assaulted and threatened by her husband, fled, hid, obtained a visa, and had her refugee claim rejected in 2015.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Federal Court decision in Huruglica guides the standard of review for RAD of RPD decisions.
Huruglica requires RAD to conduct a hybrid appeal with independent assessment and substitution of decision if differing from RPD.
RAD can respect RPD credibility findings but is not restricted to intervening only for overriding and palpable error.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Huruglica guides RAD to conduct hybrid appeals with independent assessment, respecting but not bound by RPD credibility findings.

propositions.text: Federal Court allows RAD to apply either standard of review pending final judgment on scope of appellate review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Federal Court allows RAD to apply either standard of review pending final appellate review judgment.

propositions.text: The RAD will independently assess the RPD decision and afford deference to RPD credibility findings or where RPD has advantage.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD will independently assess RPD decision, deferring to RPD credibility findings or where RPD has advantage.

propositions.text: The RPD found credibility was the determinative issue and found the Appellant not credible on central claim elements.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility determinative and found the Appellant not credible on central claim elements.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative inference from inconsistencies between testimony and CIC forms about addresses in Pakistan.
RPD rejected Appellant's explanation for inconsistencies and noted delay in refugee claim filing.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found inconsistencies in Appellant's testimony and forms, rejected her explanation, and noted delay in claim filing.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD failed to properly apply Gender Guidelines and focused on minor issues affecting credibility unreasonably.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD failed to apply Gender Guidelines and unreasonably focused on minor credibility issues.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with RPD's credibility conclusion and finds no abuse in applying Gender Guidelines.
The Appellant is educated, had an interpreter, and no psychological reports support claimed abuse effects.
The RAD does not accept Appellant's explanation for incorrect CIC information and finds cumulative credibility issues justify negative finding.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with RPD's credibility finding, finds no Gender Guidelines abuse, and rejects Appellant's explanations.

propositions.text: RPD gave little weight to note from XXXX XXXX due to Appellant's lack of credibility and absence of witness.
RPD gave little weight to letters from Appellant's father and brother due to credibility concerns and interest.
RPD discounted medical notes due to credibility concerns and prevalence of fraudulent documents in Pakistan.
Medical note about father's injuries was given little weight as it did not link injuries to Appellant's husband.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD gave little weight to supporting notes and letters due to credibility concerns and lack of disinterestedness.

propositions.text: It is a reviewable error for the Board to find an Appellant not credible and then reject supporting documents based on that.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues it is a reviewable error to find them not credible and then reject supporting documents on that basis.

propositions.text: The RAD is mindful of the use of credibility findings to discredit supporting documentation in reviewing the RPD decision.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes it is mindful of credibility findings affecting document weight in reviewing the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The letter from Imran lacks detail and source information, so it has no probative value and little weight is given to it.
The RPD's findings on this letter are thin and problematic but the reasoning is sound given other claim issues.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Imran's letter lacks detail and gives it little weight, agreeing with the RPD's reasoning despite thin findings.

propositions.text: The father's affidavit embellishes and has no probative value on the risk of death issue.
The Appellant was not present during alleged attempts and did not mention them in her narrative, suggesting embellishment.
The Appellant's testimony about threats and searches does not support the father's murder claim, which is conjecture.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the father's affidavit embellishes and lacks probative value, unsupported by the Appellant's narrative and testimony.

propositions.text: The medical note contradicts the RPD's finding but is a clinical note, not notarized, and lacks supporting medical records.
Victims of crime in Pakistan receive medical and medico-legal reports, which should have been submitted if available.
The RAD supports the RPD's finding on fraudulent documentation availability in Pakistan and gives the note no probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the medical note unsubstantiated and supports the RPD's concerns about fraudulent documents, giving it no probative value.

propositions.text: The January 2015 medical note about the Appellant's father lacks detail about the alleged perpetrator.
The four discussed documents are not probative of the Appellant's alleged fear of murder if returned to Pakistan.
Due to lack of probative documentation, the Appellant has not been credible about attempted murder allegations by her husband.
Was the RPD's credibility determination reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the documents unprobative and the Appellant not credible on attempted murder allegations, questioning the RPD's credibility finding.

propositions.text: The RPD drew a negative inference from the absence of the armed men incident in the BOC narrative.
The RPD reasoned such central events should have been included in the BOC narrative.
The Appellant said including everything would make the BOC a book.
The RPD rejected this, noting the BOC specifically asked about harm or threats to family.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the absence of key threats in the BOC narrative undermined credibility, rejecting the Appellant's explanation.

propositions.text: The RPD's findings are unreasonable, supported by four federal cases.
The BOC narrative statement about people sent in May 2014 was sufficient before hearing expansion.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD's findings are unreasonable and that the BOC narrative was sufficient initially.

propositions.text: The RAD concurs with the RPD that the alleged attack is central and not credible without BOC narrative inclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with the RPD that the alleged attack is central and not credible without BOC narrative details.

propositions.text: The RPD found it not plausible that the husband would tolerate children attending a non-Islamic school while threatening the wife.
The RPD reasoned the husband's contradictory behavior was implausible given his religious zeal and threats.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found it implausible the husband would allow children to attend a non-Islamic school given his threats and zeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD's plausibility finding is in error and that permitting school choice is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in plausibility finding and that school choice permission is reasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the RPD's finding somewhat speculative but not determinative.
The Appellant testified the husband agreed to no say in children's education and no harm to children, only to her.
The RAD finds the BOC narrative about dangerous men outside children's hostel inconsistent with testimony.
The determinative issue is whether the husband would harm the Appellant, not the children.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the RPD's finding speculative but not determinative, focusing on harm risk to the Appellant, not children.

propositions.text: The RAD determines no serious possibility of persecution or risk of torture, death, or cruel treatment if returned to Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes no serious possibility of persecution or risk if the Appellant returns to Pakistan.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision denying refugee status and protection, dismissing the appeal.
